questions.q: State the one condition a list must meet for a binary search to work.

markPoints.concept: the list must be in order
markPoints.exemplar: The list must be sorted into order.

questions.example: The list must be sorted into order.
questions.paraphrase: It has to be in order first.
questions.feedback: Sorted. Everything else about binary search follows from this.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.1 Lesson 7 — Halving hall, station 1: How it works

questions.q: Put the steps of a binary search in order.
steps: Find the middle item of the list
Compare it with the item being searched for
Discard the half that cannot contain the item
Repeat on the half that remains
questions.feedback: Middle, compare, discard half, repeat. Each step halves what is left.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.1 Lesson 7 — Halving hall, station 1: How it works

questions.q: A binary search is used on a sorted list of 8 items. In the worst case, how many comparisons are needed?
questions.feedback: 8 halves to 4, then 2, then 1: three comparisons.
questions.hint: How many times can you halve 8 before one item is left?
questions.revisitLabel: 2.1 Lesson 7 — Halving hall, station 1: How it works

questions.q: A binary search is used on a sorted list of 1,000 items. Roughly how many comparisons are needed in the worst case?
questions.feedback: Each comparison halves the list: 1000, 500, 250, 125, 63, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Ten comparisons. A linear search would need up to a thousand.
questions.hint: Keep halving 1,000 and count how many times you can do it.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.1 Lesson 7 — Halving hall, station 1: How it works

questions.q: Explain why a binary search is much faster than a linear search on a large sorted list.

markPoints.concept: a binary search discards half the remaining list at every step
accept: half the list|half of the list|half the remaining|half of what|halve the list|halves the list|half the items|half the data|discards half|throws away half|half each time|half every time|halving|50%
markPoints.exemplar: Each comparison discards half of what is left.

markPoints.concept: a linear search checks one item at a time
accept: one at a time|one by one|each item|every item|each one|item by item|one item|single item|a single
markPoints.exemplar: A linear search checks one item at a time.

markPoints.concept: so the number of comparisons grows far more slowly as the list grows
accept: fewer comparisons|far fewer|many fewer|grows slowly|grows enormously|gap grows|far more slowly|much more slowly|does not grow|much less|10|ten|hardly increases
markPoints.exemplar: So as the list gets bigger the binary search needs far fewer comparisons.

questions.example: A binary search throws away half of what remains at every comparison, while a linear search can only eliminate one item at a time. That means doubling the size of the list adds one comparison to a binary search and doubles the work for a linear search, so the gap grows enormously on a large list.
questions.paraphrase: Every check in a binary search eliminates half the remaining data, whereas a linear search removes a single item, which means the number of comparisons rises far more slowly as the list grows.
questions.feedback: Three ideas: what binary does, what linear does, and what that means as the list grows.
